question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

OBSOLETE
option_3: Prevailing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Outdated.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Obsolete (adjective) means no longer in use or no longer useful, having been replaced by something newer. (अप्रचलित, पुराना पड़ चुका)
◦ Example: The department still runs software that became obsolete a decade ago.

 

• Outdated carries exactly this sense — out of date, belonging to a time that has passed. (पुराना, समयबाह्य)
◦ Example: The manual contained outdated instructions for a machine long since scrapped.

 

• The word comes from Latin obsolescere (to fall into disuse). Note the related verb obsolesce and the noun obsolescence, as in planned obsolescence — the deliberate designing of goods to become outdated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Contemporary (समकालीन, आधुनिक): belonging to the present time — the opposite.

 

• Option 3: Prevailing (प्रचलित): currently widespread or in force — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Novel (नया, नवीन): new and unusual — again the reverse.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of obsolete asked in SSC: antiquated, archaic, defunct, outmoded, superannuated.

 

• Antonyms: current, modern, up-to-date, fashionable, prevalent.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

MUNDANE
option_3: Extraordinary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Extraordinary.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mundane (adjective) means dull, ordinary and lacking interest; concerned with the everyday rather than the remarkable. (सांसारिक, सामान्य)
◦ Example: Most of his day was spent on mundane clerical tasks.

 

• Extraordinary means far beyond what is usual or expected, and is therefore its direct opposite. (असाधारण)
◦ Example: The rescue called for extraordinary presence of mind.

 

• The word comes from Latin mundus (the world), so its older sense is “of this world”, as opposed to the spiritual — a sense that survives in phrases such as mundane affairs.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Ordinary (सामान्य): usual, with nothing special about it — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Routine (नियमित, घिसा-पिटा): done as part of a regular procedure — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Commonplace (साधारण): so frequent as to be uninteresting — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Three options agree and one stands apart — the odd option is the answer. Other antonyms of mundane: exceptional, remarkable, exotic, singular, sublime.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

TURBULENT
option_3: Chaotic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tranquil.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Turbulent (adjective) means disturbed, violently disordered or marked by conflict — used of water, weather, times or emotions. (अशांत, उथल-पुथल भरा)
◦ Example: The region passed through a turbulent decade before the accord was signed.

 

• Tranquil means calm, peaceful and free from disturbance, and is therefore its direct opposite. (शांत)
◦ Example: The lake was tranquil in the early hours of the morning.

 

• The word comes from Latin turba (a crowd, a commotion), the same root as disturb and turmoil.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Stormy (तूफानी): marked by storms or violent feeling — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Chaotic (अराजक, अव्यवस्थित): in complete disorder — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Agitated (उत्तेजित, व्याकुल): troubled and restless — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of turbulent: serene, placid, still, composed, unruffled. Note that placid and serene are commonly set as options in the same question.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

A storm in a teacup
option_1: Great excitement or anger over a trivial matter
option_2: A quarrel that destroys a lasting friendship
option_3: A disaster that arrives without any warning
option_4: A private plan discussed among a few people
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Great excitement or anger over a trivial matter.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “A storm in a teacup” means a great deal of fuss, outrage or anxiety about something unimportant. (राई का पहाड़ बनाना)
◦ Example: The controversy over the seating arrangement turned out to be a storm in a teacup.

 

• The image itself carries the meaning — a storm, which suggests violence, confined to a teacup, which suggests triviality. The disproportion between the two is the whole point of the idiom.

 

• The American form of the same idiom is “a tempest in a teapot”.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes a serious rupture, which would be “a parting of ways” — the idiom implies the opposite, that nothing much was at stake.

 

• Option 3 describes a sudden calamity — “a bolt from the blue”.

 

• Option 4 describes secret consultation — “a closed-door meeting”.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of exaggeration frequently tested: to make a mountain out of a molehill, much ado about nothing, to blow something out of proportion, to cry wolf.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To turn a blind eye
option_1: To pretend not to notice something wrong
option_2: To lose one’s temper without warning
option_3: To refuse to give evidence in court
option_4: To search for something with great care
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To pretend not to notice something wrong.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To turn a blind eye” means to deliberately ignore something one knows to be wrong, choosing not to act on it. (जानबूझकर अनदेखी करना)
◦ Example: The inspectors turned a blind eye to the overloading of trucks for years.

 

• The essential element is that the person knows and still chooses not to see; mere failure to notice would not be described by this idiom.

 

• The phrase is popularly traced to Admiral Nelson, who is said to have raised a telescope to his blind eye at Copenhagen and declared that he could not see the signal ordering him to withdraw.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes sudden anger — “to fly off the handle”.

 

• Option 3 describes silence in court, for which the idiom would be “to take the Fifth” in American usage; the given idiom has no legal sense.

 

• Option 4 describes a careful search — “to leave no stone unturned”.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of the eye: to keep an eye on (to watch), to see eye to eye (to agree), an eye for an eye (retaliation), to catch someone’s eye (to attract attention).

question: Which is the correct spelling of a word meaning ‘rule by the wealthy’?
option_3: Plutoccracy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Plutocracy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Plutocracy means government by the wealthy, or a class that rules by virtue of its wealth. (धनतंत्र)
◦ Example: Critics warned that unregulated funding of elections would turn the republic into a plutocracy.

 

• The spelling follows the Greek elements ploutos (wealth) + kratia (rule): pluto- + -cracy. Every word of this family ends in -cracy, with a c, never -crasy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Plutocrasy — an ‘s’ wrongly replaces the ‘c’ of -cracy.

 

• Option 3: Plutoccracy — the ‘c’ has been doubled without reason.

 

• Option 4: Plootocracy — a phonetic spelling of the first element; the root is pluto-.

 

NOTE

 

• Learn the family together: autocracy (rule by one), aristocracy (rule by a privileged class), bureaucracy (rule by officials), theocracy (rule by priests), meritocracy (rule by the able), kleptocracy (rule by thieves), ochlocracy (rule by the mob).

question: Spot the correct spelling of the wave-like muscular movement that pushes food along the alimentary canal.
option_3: Peristalsys
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Peristalsis.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Peristalsis is the rhythmic wave of muscular contraction and relaxation that moves food through the digestive tract. (क्रमाकुंचन)
◦ Example: Peristalsis carries the swallowed food down the oesophagus even against gravity.

 

• The word is built from Greek peri- (around) + stalsis (contraction). Fixing the two parts settles the spelling as peri- + stalsis, with an ‘i’ in the prefix and the ending -sis, the usual suffix for a bodily process.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Perastalsis — the prefix is peri-, not pera-.

 

• Option 3: Peristalsys — the ending must be -sis; -sys is not an English suffix.

 

• Option 4: Perisalsis — the ‘t’ of stalsis has been dropped.

 

NOTE

 

• The prefix peri- (around) recurs in perimeter, periscope, periphery, pericardium (the membrane around the heart) and perigee (the point nearest the earth).

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: ‘A person who cannot be corrected or reformed’.
option_3: Invincible
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Incorrigible.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Incorrigible means beyond correction or reform; used of a person whose bad habits cannot be cured. (सुधारा न जा सकने वाला)
◦ Example: He was an incorrigible gossip, warned a dozen times and never once deterred.

 

• The word is formed from in- (not) + corrigere (to correct), the same root as correct and corrigendum (a correction to be made in a printed text).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Irreparable (अपूरणीय): impossible to repair or make good — used of damage or loss, not of a person’s character.

 

• Option 3: Invincible (अजेय): impossible to defeat.

 

• Option 4: Intractable (असाध्य, हठी): hard to control or to solve; close in feeling, but it describes difficulty of management, not the impossibility of reform.

 

NOTE

 

• The negative-prefix family is a standing favourite: illegible (cannot be read), inaudible (cannot be heard), indelible (cannot be erased), inevitable (cannot be avoided), inexorable (cannot be persuaded), impregnable (cannot be captured).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

 ‘A narrow strip of land joining two larger landmasses’.
option_3: Archipelago
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Isthmus.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An isthmus is a narrow neck of land connecting two larger areas of land, with water on either side. (स्थलडमरूमध्य)
◦ Example: The Isthmus of Panama joins North America to South America.

 

• Note the two essentials in the definition — the land is narrow, and it joins two larger landmasses. Any option lacking either element must be rejected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Peninsula (प्रायद्वीप): a piece of land almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland — it projects, it does not connect two landmasses.

 

• Option 3: Archipelago (द्वीपसमूह): a group or chain of islands.

 

• Option 4: Strait (जलडमरूमध्य): a narrow channel of water joining two larger seas — the exact counterpart of an isthmus, and the commonest distractor with it.

 

NOTE

 

• Other geographical terms set in such questions: estuary (the tidal mouth of a river), delta (a triangular deposit at a river mouth), lagoon (shallow water separated by a sandbar), fjord (a deep inlet between cliffs), plateau (elevated flat land).

question:
Choose the correct phrasal verb:

 

The auditors could not ____ the discrepancy between the two sets of figures.
option_3: stand for
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. account for.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ‘To account for’ means to explain the cause or reason for something, or to give a satisfactory record of it.
◦ Complete sentence: The auditors could not account for the discrepancy between the two sets of figures.
◦ Example: The report failed to account for the sudden rise in expenditure.

 

• The object here is a discrepancy, which is precisely the kind of thing one is called upon to explain — the strongest clue in the sentence.

 

• The same phrasal verb has a second common sense: to form a part of a total — Agriculture accounts for a large share of employment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘count on’ means to rely upon — We are counting on your support.

 

• Option 3: ‘stand for’ means to represent or to tolerate — UNO stands for the United Nations Organisation.

 

• Option 4: ‘fall for’ means to be deceived by, or to fall in love with — He fell for the trick at once.

 

NOTE

 

• Phrasal verbs on account, call and carry recur in SSC: call off (to cancel), call for (to demand), carry out (to execute), carry on (to continue), carry over (to postpone to a later period).

question:
Select the correct option:

 

She answered every objection so ____ that the panel was left with no doubt at all.
option_3: convincingly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. convincingly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank describes how she answered — it modifies the verb answered, and a word that modifies a verb must be an adverb. The adverb form here is convincingly.
◦ Complete sentence: She answered every objection so convincingly that the panel was left with no doubt at all.

 

• The structure ‘so + adverb + that’ is the second clue. When the word after so qualifies a verb, it takes -ly; only when so is followed by a linking verb (is, seems, appears) does an adjective follow — Her reply was so convincing that …

 

• Compare the pair carefully:
◦ She spoke convincingly. (adverb with an action verb)
◦ Her argument was convincing. (adjective after a linking verb)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘convince’ is the verb; a second finite verb cannot stand here.

 

• Option 2: ‘convincing’ is the adjective, which would need a noun or a linking verb to attach to.

 

• Option 4: ‘convincingness’ is an awkward noun form and cannot follow so in this pattern.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the irregular adverbs that SSC tests: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard (hardly means ‘scarcely’), late → late (lately means ‘recently’), near → near (nearly means ‘almost’).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The floodwaters had (1)/ rised well above the danger mark (2)/ by the time the relief teams (3)/ reached the outlying villages. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rise is an irregular verb: rise – rose – risen. There is no such form as rised. After the auxiliary had, the verb must take its third form, giving had risen.
◦ Corrected: The floodwaters had risen well above the danger mark by the time the relief teams reached the outlying villages.

 

• Distinguish rise from raise, which is regular and transitive: raise – raised – raised. Water rises by itself; a person raises something.
◦ The river rose overnight. / They raised the embankment.

 

• The past perfect is correctly used, since the water had risen before the teams arrived; only the participle is at fault.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: had is the right auxiliary for the earlier of two past actions.

 

• Part (3) is correct: by the time introduces a clause of time.

 

• Part (4) is correct: the simple past reached marks the later action.

 

NOTE

 

• Irregular pairs that SSC repeatedly confuses: lie – lay – lain (to recline) against lay – laid – laid (to place); sit – sat – sat against set – set – set; fall – fell – fallen against fell – felled – felled (to cut down).

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

Someone should have informed the passengers about the change of platform.
option_1: The passengers should be informed about the change of platform.
option_2: The passengers should have been informed about the change of platform.
option_3: The passengers should have informed about the change of platform.
option_4: The passengers must have been informed by someone about the change of platform.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The passengers should have been informed about the change of platform.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active verb is a perfect modal, should have informed. Its passive is formed as:
◦ Object + modal + have been + V3.

 

• Applying the rule: the passengers becomes the subject, and should have informed becomes should have been informed. The modal should is never altered in the passive.

 

• The vague agent someone is dropped in the passive, as is normal when the doer is unknown or unimportant — by someone would add nothing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the simple modal passive should be informed, which points to the present or future and loses the sense of a duty already neglected.

 

• Option 3 omits been, leaving an active form with a passive meaning — as written, it says the passengers did the informing.

 

• Option 4 replaces should with must, changing an unfulfilled obligation into a confident conclusion.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare the two modal passives: modal + be + V3 (The form may be signed today) and modal + have been + V3 (The form may have been signed yesterday). The first looks forward; the second looks back.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The headmaster praised the pupil for her patience and diligence.
option_1: The brightest pupil in the class was awarded a scholarship.
option_2: The doctor shone a light to check the pupil of his left eye.
option_3: Every pupil of the school attended the annual function.
option_4: She had been his pupil for nearly four years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The doctor shone a light to check the pupil of his left eye.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, pupil means a student taught by a teacher. (विद्यार्थी, शिष्य)

 

• In Option 2, pupil is the dark circular opening at the centre of the iris of the eye, through which light passes. (पुतली) That is a wholly different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The two meanings share an origin in Latin pupilla (a little doll) — the tiny reflected figure one sees in another person’s eye — but in modern English they are treated as distinct words.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: the brightest pupil in the class — a student; identical in meaning to the highlighted word.

 

• Option 3: every pupil of the school — again a student.

 

• Option 4: his pupil for four years — the same sense once more.

 

NOTE

 

• Other homonyms of this kind, where a body part shares its name with something else: iris (part of the eye / a flower), palm (part of the hand / a tree), temple (side of the head / a place of worship), sole (of the foot / a fish).

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The approach road was being widened by the contractors when the rains arrived.
option_1: The contractors widened the approach road when the rains arrived.
option_2: The contractors had widened the approach road when the rains arrived.
option_3: The contractors were widening the approach road when the rains arrived.
option_4: The approach road widened as the contractors worked before the rains.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The contractors were widening the approach road when the rains arrived.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The agent introduced by by — the contractors — becomes the subject, and the passive subject the approach road becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb was being widened is in the past continuous, so the active verb must also be past continuous → were widening (plural, agreeing with the contractors).
◦ Active: The contractors were widening the approach road when the rains arrived.

 

• The rule for continuous tenses: was/were being + V3 (passive) ↔ was/were + V-ing (active). The word being disappears in the active voice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts to the simple past, which turns an action in progress into a completed one.

 

• Option 2 uses the past perfect, implying the work was already finished before the rains — the reverse of the original meaning.

 

• Option 4 rewrites the sentence altogether and makes the road widen by itself.

 

NOTE

 

• Only four tenses form a natural passive with being or been: present continuous, past continuous, and the perfect tenses. The future continuous and perfect continuous tenses are avoided in the passive because the forms become clumsy.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Privacy is commonly defended as the right to keep secrets, and that defence, though not wrong, is too narrow to be of much use. What privacy actually protects is the capacity to be different things in different settings — a colleague at work, a child at home, an amateur among strangers — and to decide for oneself which version of a life a given audience may see. When that control is lost, it is not merely information that leaks; it is the ability to hold a self together across contexts. The familiar retort — that a person with nothing to hide has nothing to fear — mistakes the nature of the loss. Surveillance does its work not chiefly by exposure but by anticipation. A citizen who knows that her searches, her movements and her conversations are recorded begins, almost imperceptibly, to trim them: she consults fewer unpopular sources, attends fewer contentious meetings, asks fewer awkward questions. This chilling effect is hard to measure precisely because it consists of things that never happen. Nor is consent the safeguard it is taken to be. A person who accepts the terms of a service has rarely read them and could not, in practice, refuse them, since the service has become a condition of ordinary employment or civic life; consent given in such circumstances records compliance rather than choice. And information surrendered for one purpose seldom stays there. Data gathered to route traffic or to detect fraud is later reassigned to policing, to insurance or to credit scoring, by institutions the individual never dealt with and cannot question. The remedy most often proposed — that people should simply be more careful — places the burden exactly where it cannot be borne, for individuals cannot audit systems they are not permitted to see. What is required instead is a design principle, enforceable in law: that data be collected only for a stated purpose, retained only as long as that purpose lasts, and never quietly reassigned. Privacy, so understood, is less a wall than a set of rules about traffic — not the concealment of a life, but the governance of what may be done with what is known about it.

 

According to the passage, what is the chief effect of surveillance on ordinary citizens?
option_1: They begin to restrain their own conduct in anticipation of being watched
option_2: They immediately demand stronger laws from the government
option_3: They lose all interest in public affairs
option_4: They learn to conceal serious wrongdoing more skilfully
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. They begin to restrain their own conduct in anticipation of being watched.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states plainly that surveillance works not chiefly by exposure but by anticipation: knowing that her searches, movements and conversations are recorded, the citizen begins almost imperceptibly to trim them.

 

• The examples given are all of self-restraint — fewer unpopular sources consulted, fewer contentious meetings attended, fewer awkward questions asked. The author names this the chilling effect, and adds that it is hard to measure because it consists of things that never happen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes a public demand that the passage nowhere reports.

 

• Option 3 overstates the case; withdrawal from a few activities is not a loss of all interest.

 

• Option 4 revives the “nothing to hide” assumption that the passage explicitly rejects.

 

NOTE

 

• In “according to the passage” questions, prefer the option that restates a line of the text. Options that sound reasonable in general but are absent from the passage are the standard traps.

Why does the author mention traffic routing and fraud detection?
option_1: To praise the efficiency of modern data systems
option_2: To show that data gathered for one purpose is later reassigned to another
option_3: To argue that financial fraud is steadily increasing
option_4: To recommend that more data be collected for public safety
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To show that data gathered for one purpose is later reassigned to another.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The two examples appear immediately after the claim that information surrendered for one purpose seldom stays there. They are therefore illustrations of that claim, not points in their own right.

 

• The passage completes the illustration by naming where such data ends up — policing, insurance and credit scoring — and adds the sting: this is done by institutions the individual never dealt with and cannot question.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the author’s purpose; the examples are offered as a warning, not as praise.

 

• Option 3 treats an example as a subject in its own right; the passage makes no claim about the level of fraud.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the closing recommendation, which is to limit collection to a stated purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• When a question asks why an example is mentioned, look at the sentence immediately before it. An example almost always supports the claim that precedes it.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. It records compliance rather than genuine choice.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage gives two reasons why consent fails as a safeguard: the user has rarely read the terms, and could not in practice refuse them, because the service has become a condition of ordinary employment or civic life.

 

• The conclusion is stated in the text itself — consent given in such circumstances records compliance rather than choice. A choice made where refusal is not possible is not really a choice at all.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the very belief the paragraph sets out to dismantle; reading the terms changes nothing if refusal is impossible.

 

• Option 2 overstates the argument — the passage questions the value of such consent, not its legal standing.

 

• Option 4 inverts the conclusion, which is that a design principle enforceable in law must do the work consent cannot.

 

NOTE

 

• An implication is what follows from what is stated, without being spelt out as a heading. Options that are too absolute (“every circumstance”, “complete safeguard”) rarely survive comparison with the text.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Privacy is commonly defended as the right to keep secrets, and that defence, though not wrong, is too narrow to be of much use. What privacy actually protects is the capacity to be different things in different settings — a colleague at work, a child at home, an amateur among strangers — and to decide for oneself which version of a life a given audience may see. When that control is lost, it is not merely information that leaks; it is the ability to hold a self together across contexts. The familiar retort — that a person with nothing to hide has nothing to fear — mistakes the nature of the loss. Surveillance does its work not chiefly by exposure but by anticipation. A citizen who knows that her searches, her movements and her conversations are recorded begins, almost imperceptibly, to trim them: she consults fewer unpopular sources, attends fewer contentious meetings, asks fewer awkward questions. This chilling effect is hard to measure precisely because it consists of things that never happen. Nor is consent the safeguard it is taken to be. A person who accepts the terms of a service has rarely read them and could not, in practice, refuse them, since the service has become a condition of ordinary employment or civic life; consent given in such circumstances records compliance rather than choice. And information surrendered for one purpose seldom stays there. Data gathered to route traffic or to detect fraud is later reassigned to policing, to insurance or to credit scoring, by institutions the individual never dealt with and cannot question. The remedy most often proposed — that people should simply be more careful — places the burden exactly where it cannot be borne, for individuals cannot audit systems they are not permitted to see. What is required instead is a design principle, enforceable in law: that data be collected only for a stated purpose, retained only as long as that purpose lasts, and never quietly reassigned. Privacy, so understood, is less a wall than a set of rules about traffic — not the concealment of a life, but the governance of what may be done with what is known about it.

 

How does the passage describe the suggestion that individuals should simply be more careful?
option_1: As the most practical solution presently available
option_2: As a remedy that places the burden where it cannot be borne
option_3: As a principle already enforced by law in most countries
option_4: As a way of making consent more meaningful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. As a remedy that places the burden where it cannot be borne.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author calls this “the remedy most often proposed” and rejects it in the same breath: it places the burden exactly where it cannot be borne, since individuals cannot audit systems they are not permitted to see.

 

• The rejection is what makes room for the alternative that follows — a design principle, enforceable in law, governing collection, retention and reassignment of data.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 states the opposite of the author’s verdict.

 

• Option 3 confuses the rejected suggestion with the legal principle the author actually recommends, which is presented as still to be adopted.

 

• Option 4 links personal caution to consent, a connection the passage never makes.

 

NOTE

 

• Phrases such as “the remedy most often proposed”, “the familiar retort” and “it is commonly said” almost always introduce a view the writer is about to reject. Reading a line further usually gives the answer.

What tone best describes the author’s stance on privacy?
option_3: Playful and ironic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Reasoned and critical.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage proceeds by argument rather than by outcry: it states a common defence of privacy, shows why it is too narrow, examines the “nothing to hide” retort, tests consent, and closes with a concrete proposal. That orderly movement is what makes the tone reasoned.

 

• It is at the same time critical, since every position it examines — secrecy, consent, personal caution — is found wanting, and the practices it describes are treated as a real danger.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Alarmed and despairing would require the author to see no way out; instead a clear remedy is proposed at the end.

 

• Option 3: Playful and ironic is ruled out by the sustained seriousness of the writing.

 

• Option 4: Detached and uninvolved cannot describe a passage that recommends a change in the law.

 

NOTE

 

• Tone questions are answered by how something is written, not by what it is about. A serious subject may be treated lightly, and the presence of a constructive proposal almost always rules out despair.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The officer explained me the procedure in considerable detail.
option_3: explained to me about the procedure
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. explained the procedure to me.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Explain does not take a person as its direct object. The pattern is explain + something + to + somebody, so the correct form is explained the procedure to me.
◦ Corrected: The officer explained the procedure to me in considerable detail.

 

• Nor does explain take about: one explains a matter, not about a matter.

 

• Contrast this with tell, which does take a person directly — He told me the procedure — and with say, which needs to — He said to me …

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the person as the direct object and adds a superfluous about.

 

• Option 3 places to me correctly but retains the unnecessary about.

 

• Option 4 changes the tense while leaving the faulty pattern untouched.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs that follow the same ‘something to somebody’ pattern: explain, describe, suggest, announce, introduce, mention, propose, report, dictate. Verbs that take the person directly: tell, inform, assure, remind, convince, notify.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

The scenery of the hill station are very beautiful in the month of October.
option_3: have been very beautiful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. is very beautiful.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Scenery is an uncountable, singular noun meaning the general appearance of a landscape. It has no plural form and therefore takes a singular verb.
◦ Corrected: The scenery of the hill station is very beautiful in the month of October.

 

• When the natural features are to be counted, English uses a countable word instead — sights, views or landscapes: The views from the ridge are magnificent.

 

• The plural-looking phrase of the hill station has no bearing on the verb; agreement is always with the head noun, here scenery.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps a plural verb and needlessly shifts the sentence into the past.

 

• Option 3 is plural and also changes the meaning to a state continuing from earlier.

 

• Option 4 merely disturbs the word order; beautiful very is not English.

 

NOTE

 

• Uncountable nouns that look plural or are wrongly pluralised in exams: scenery, machinery, furniture, luggage, poetry, jewellery, stationery, information, advice, equipment. None of them takes -s or a plural verb.

question:
Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below.

 

He warned that if the monsoon failed again, the reservoir would run dry before April.
option_1: He said, “If the monsoon fails again, the reservoir will run dry before April.”
option_2: He said, “If the monsoon failed again, the reservoir would run dry before April.”
option_3: He said, “Had the monsoon failed again, the reservoir would have run dry before April.”
option_4: He said, “The reservoir will run dry before April if the monsoon would fail again.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He said, “If the monsoon fails again, the reservoir will run dry before April.”

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence uses the first conditional back-shifted by the past reporting verb warned. Converting to direct speech means undoing that back-shift:
◦ failed returns to fails;
◦ would run returns to will run.

 

• The result is the ordinary first conditional, which states a real future possibility: If + simple present, … will + V1.
◦ Direct: He said, “If the monsoon fails again, the reservoir will run dry before April.”

 

• Inverted commas, the capital letter and the original tense must all be restored; the connective that is dropped.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 simply reproduces the reported forms inside inverted commas, so no conversion has taken place.

 

• Option 3 turns the sentence into a third conditional, which would describe an unreal past — quite a different meaning.

 

• Option 4 places would inside the if-clause, which is not permitted in a conditional sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Conditionals in reported speech: first conditional back-shifts to if + past, would + V1; second and third conditionals do not change at all, because they are already unreal.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

She said, “I have finished the assignment.”
option_1: She said that she has finished the assignment.
option_2: She said that she had finished the assignment.
option_3: She said that she finished the assignment.
option_4: She said that she was finishing the assignment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She said that she had finished the assignment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb said is in the past, so the reported speech must be back-shifted one step. The present perfect (have finished) becomes the past perfect (had finished).

 

• The pronoun I becomes she, the connective that is added, and the inverted commas are removed.
◦ Indirect: She said that she had finished the assignment.

 

• Note that both the present perfect and the simple past move to the past perfect in reported speech, which is why option 3 is not an acceptable substitute.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves the present perfect unchanged after a past reporting verb.

 

• Option 3 uses the simple past, which fails to show that the action was complete before the moment of reporting.

 

• Option 4 turns a completed action into one still in progress, altering the meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Back-shift at a glance: simple present → simple past; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; simple past → past perfect; past perfect → unchanged. Universal truths and habitual facts remain unchanged.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The word ‘quarantine’ preserves within it a fragment of medieval public health practice.

 

A. Ships from suspect ports were therefore held at anchor for the full term before anyone was allowed ashore.

 

B. It comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning forty days.

 

C. What began as a precaution against plague has thus left its arithmetic behind in the language.

 

D. Venetian authorities settled on that period during the years when plague travelled along their trade routes.

 

S2. Six centuries later the same word still governs what happens at a border during an epidemic.
option_3: B-D-A-C
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from claim → derivation → historical setting → practice → conclusion.

 

• S1 makes the claim that the word carries a piece of history within it.
◦ B supplies the derivation, and the pronoun It at its head points straight back to the word in S1.
◦ D speaks of “that period”, a phrase that can only mean the forty days named in B, so D must follow it.
◦ A begins with “therefore” and refers to “the full term”, describing the practice that resulted from the rule fixed in D.
◦ C sums the episode up (What began as … has thus left …) and leads naturally into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) allows ships to be held for “the full term” before any term has been fixed.

 

• Option 2 (D-B-A-C) opens with “that period”, which has not yet been mentioned.

 

• Option 4 (D-A-B-C) places the derivation in the middle, after the practice it is meant to explain.

 

NOTE

 

• Three signposts settle this question: a pronoun (It) must follow its noun, a demonstrative (that period) must follow what it points to, and a connective (therefore) must follow the fact it draws upon.
